keyframe_review.note: The Commandancy General of the Provincias Internas, 'formally created in 1776', groups Sonora, Sinaloa, Nueva Vizcaya, the Californias, Coahuila, Texas, New Mexico, New León and New Santander (the whole north), still nominally under the viceroy. Drawn as Mexico of 1790 (Cliopatria) plus New Mexico, Texas and the Californias. The New Spain page claims at the 'greatest extent' also the Floridas, Louisiana, the Caribbean islands and the Philippines: those are in separate dossiers (Spanish Louisiana, the Captaincy General of Guatemala) or in the Spanish Empire's.

region.text: Cliopatria's Spanish Empire shape of 1534 within modern Mexico, without Chiapas (Captaincy General of Guatemala)

ledger.note: 1535 (12 October): the Viceroyalty of New Spain is created at Mexico City. 'The Viceroyalty of New Spain was created by royal decree on 12 October 1535.' The Kingdom of New Spain dated from 18 August 1521. The page gives no boundary; the core is drawn from Cliopatria's Spanish Empire shape of 1534 in Mexico.

region.text: the western kingdom of Nueva Galicia, seat of the Audiencia of Guadalajara

ledger.note: 1548: the Audiencia of Guadalajara is set up for Nueva Galicia. The page lists 'Guadalajara (1548)' among the audiencias; it does not say when Nueva Galicia was conquered, nor who held it.

region.text: Santa Fe de Nuevo Mexico, 'centered on the upper valley of the Rio Grande'

ledger.note: 1598 (12 July): Oñate founds the colony of Santa Fe de Nuevo Mexico. 'On July 12, 1598, Oñate established the New Spain colony of Santa Fe de Nuevo Méjico'; the capital was first San Juan de los Caballeros, and Santa Fe was founded by Peralta in 1610. The colony was 'centered on the upper valley of the Rio Grande'; the gazetteer region over-states the settled land.

region.text: Santa Fe de Nuevo Mexico, 'centered on the upper valley of the Rio Grande'

ledger.note: 1680: the Pueblo Revolt expels the Spanish from New Mexico. 'This rebellion saw the Spanish expelled from Nuevo México for a period of 12 years.' The page dates the revolt only to 1680.

region.text: Santa Fe de Nuevo Mexico, 'centered on the upper valley of the Rio Grande'

ledger.note: 1692: the Spanish return to New Mexico after twelve years. The page says the Spanish were out 'for a period of 12 years' (1680 to 1692), that 'In 1692 the province fell under the Real Audiencia de Guadalajara', and that Diego de Vargas reoccupied Santa Fe; it does not give the month.

region.text: East Texas between the Sabine and the Red River

ledger.note: 1716: Texas becomes a buffer against French Louisiana. Spain 'ordered the reoccupation of Texas as a buffer between French settlements in Louisiana and New Spain'; Spain 'claimed that the Red River formed the boundary' while France 'insisted that the border was the Sabine River'. The page also has St. Denis agree in 1721 to 'abandon East Texas and return to Louisiana'.

region.text: the province of Texas, the East Texas missions and San Antonio

ledger.note: 1716 (12 April): Spain reoccupies East Texas. 'On April 12, 1716, an expedition led by Domingo Ramón left San Juan Bautista for Texas', reestablishing the East Texas missions; Los Adaes became the first capital in 1721 and San Antonio in 1772. The first missions (San Francisco de los Tejas, 1690) had been abandoned in 1693.

region.text: East Texas between the Sabine and the Red River

ledger.note: 1762 (3 November): the dispute over East Texas ends with the cession of Louisiana. 'Under the Treaty of Fontainebleau (signed November 3, 1762), France ceded the portion of Louisiana west of the Mississippi River to Spain'; the Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1763 confirmed it.

region.text: 'occupy and fortify San Diego and Monterey' (1768 order)

ledger.note: 1768: the order to occupy California. 'In 1768, Gálvez received the order to' occupy and fortify San Diego and Monterey. The page does not give the year of the occupation itself.

region.text: the Californias, in the 1776 Commandancy General plan

ledger.note: 1776: the Californias join the Commandancy General of the Provincias Internas. The Commandancy 'was formally created in 1776' (royal instructions of 22 August 1776, Teodoro de Croix first commander) over the north-west frontier; Sonora, Sinaloa, Nueva Vizcaya and the Californias were in the 1768 plan. Baja and Alta California are drawn whole from here; the page gives no earlier dates for the northern provinces, which Cliopatria's Spanish Empire shape already holds to 31.8 N by 1700.

union.text: the Neutral Ground between the Sabine and Arroyo Hondo

region.text: the eastern Texas frontier and the Neutral Ground

ledger.note: 1803: the Louisiana Purchase puts the United States on the Texas border. 'After the Louisiana Purchase in 1803, the United States asserted claims to an imprecisely defined area that included parts of Texas.' A 1806 agreement left the land between the Sabine River and Arroyo Hondo neutral ground, which 'quickly became a haven for lawlessness'.

region.text: the insurgent-held land as Cliopatria draws it

ledger.note: 1810: the Mexican War of Independence begins. The page gives 'the Mexican War of Independence, 1810–1821' after Hidalgo's 1810 Cry of Dolores, an 'eleven-year war against Spanish rule'. The zone is Cliopatria's insurgent shape of 1811; the page names no territory.

region.text: the eastern Texas frontier and the Neutral Ground

ledger.note: 1819 (22 February): the Adams-Onís Treaty fixes the northern boundary. Signed 22 February 1819, in force 22 February 1821; the line follows the Sabine to 32 N, due north to the Red River, the Red to 100 W, north to the Arkansas, its southern bank to the source, then the 42nd parallel to the Pacific; Spain also cedes East and West Florida and 'withdrew historic claims to the Oregon Country'.

region.text: the insurgent-held land as Cliopatria draws it

ledger.note: 1821: the war ends with Mexican independence. 'In 1821, New Spain officially became the independent nation of Mexico, ending three centuries of Spanish colonial rule.' The page names Iturbide's alliance with the insurgent Vicente Guerrero but gives no month.

ledger.note: 1821: New Spain ends in Mexican independence. 'At its conclusion in 1821, the viceroyalty was dissolved and the Mexican Empire was established.' The northern provinces followed: Texas 'became a part of the newly independent nation without a shot being fired' (Texas page) and Baja California's governor acceded in 1822 (Provincias Internas page).

wars.name: Mexican War of Independence
wars.outcome: Independence: 'In 1821, New Spain officially became the independent nation of Mexico'; the viceroyalty was dissolved and the Mexican Empire established.
wars.note: The page names the war and its dates but no campaigns or territories; the zone is taken from Cliopatria's 'Mexicans' shapes (1811-1819).

wars.name: Pueblo Revolt

zones.text: Santa Fe de Nuevo Mexico, 'centered on the upper valley of the Rio Grande'

wars.outcome: The Pueblo peoples drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for twelve years; Spanish rule was restored in 1692.

wars.name: Spanish reoccupation of East Texas (against French Louisiana)
wars.outcome: Spain reoccupied the East Texas missions in 1716 as a buffer; the French agent St. Denis agreed in 1721 to abandon East Texas. The Sabine/Red River dispute lasted until the 1762 cession of Louisiana.

wars.name: Louisiana Purchase boundary dispute (Texas and the Neutral Ground)
wars.outcome: No war: a Neutral Ground between the Sabine and Arroyo Hondo from 1806; the Adams-Onís Treaty of 22 February 1819 fixed the Sabine boundary.

certainty.note: Colonial frontiers are lines of settlement, mission and presidio, not surveyed borders; the northern and Pacific frontiers of New Spain are approximate throughout.
The boundary with the United States (Sabine, Red River, 100 W, Arkansas, 42 N) is fixed by the Adams-Onís Treaty of 22 February 1819, in force 22 February 1821; every other frontier stays soft.

notes:
Written by am-06-x from five pages (budget 2-5). Not settled:
(1) Extent before 1776: the New Spain page gives no area and no boundary; keyframes 1535-1775 take Cliopatria's Spanish Empire shape inside Mexico (minus Chiapas) as the base and add only what a page dates (Nueva Galicia 1548, New Mexico 1598/1680/1692, Texas 1716, the Californian ports 1768). The conquests of Michoacan, Oaxaca, Yucatan, Nueva Vizcaya, Nuevo Leon, Coahuila, Sonora and Sinaloa are not dated by any page opened; a gap-filler should open the pages of those provinces.
(2) Overlaps by design: the New Spain page says the viceroyalty also had jurisdiction over Central America (the Captaincy General of Guatemala, here its own dossier), Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, the Floridas, Louisiana (a 'province of New Spain from 1762 to 1801', Louisiana page; separate dossier spanish-louisiana) and the Philippines and Guam (Philippines '1565' in one list and 'established 1574' in another on the same page). Those are left out of this shape so that the map does not draw two colours on one cell; the reviewer may prefer to draw them as New Spain dependencies.
(3) Dates the pages disagree on: the Provincias Internas page says 1776 for the Commandancy and the Santa Fe page 1777.
(4) No area figure on any page for the viceroyalty, so Cliopatria's areas could not be compared. The Santa Fe page's 603,345 km2 is the Mexican territory of 1842, not the colony.
(5) Counterparts needing a dossier: pueblo-revolt (Pueblo peoples, 1680-1692; also suggested by am-06-b). Gazetteer: all region names resolved at write time.
(6) Months not given by the pages are left out; the end month of 1821 is not on the pages opened (the Treaty of Cordoba date is on a page another group opened).
